paras: The lynching of Mike Wells was the hanging of a Black man by a mob in the Court House yard at Dyersburg, Dyer County, Tennessee, on August 1, 1881. Wells had been arrested on an accusation of attempting to outrage a widow, Mrs. Childs, and was said to have confessed before the mob took him from his guard. The wire report ran in papers across the country, and later that month Governor Hawkins offered a $5,000 reward for the conviction of the men who had mobbed him.

According to a special from Rutherford, Tennessee, printed in the Memphis Daily Appeal, Wells, described as "colored," entered the house of Mrs. Childs, "widow of J. F. Childs," between 12 and 1 o'clock on Sunday night, the night before the lynching. The Appeal said he choked her until she raised an alarm, which drove him off and brought a young man who roomed nearby. The shorter wire account said only that he "attempted to commit an outrage" and fled, frightened by her shrieks; the Stark County Democrat's version added that he escaped by jumping through a window.

Wells was tracked by his footprints, which the wire said were made by feet "encased in sacks full of holes" ("socks" in other printings). The Appeal reported that the police, headed by Ex-Sheriff Nichols, arrested him by 4 o'clock Monday morning and placed him under guard. Every account states that he confessed, a claim that comes from the reports alone.

Between 10 and 11 o'clock, according to the Appeal, "an indignant mob" took possession of him and hanged him from a limb in the Courthouse yard. The wire instead said he was hanged "by the citizens" in the Court House yard between twelve and one o'clock in the morning, and the Stark County Democrat called them "a mob of citizens of the town." None of the reports gives the size of the mob or names any of its members.

No report of an inquest or of any arrest of the lynchers appears in the coverage. At the end of August, Governor Hawkins of Tennessee offered $5,000 "for all, or any one or more, of the persons who mobbed Mike Wells, in Dyer county, August 1, 1881." The same proclamation offered equal rewards in the Murfreesboro and Lake County cases. The Morristown Gazette introduced the list by saying the governor "is determined to make an effort to put a stop to mob law," and the Milan Exchange noted the reward for "parties engaged in the same thing at Dyersburg."

The Dyersburg dispatch reached papers from Maine to Georgia within two days, usually as a few lines under headings such as "A Culprit Lynched," "A Negro Lynched," and "Judge Lynch in Tennessee." These reprints presented the accusation and the confession as fact, and the People and New Hampshire Patriot headed its version "A Villain Hanged by the People." Weekly digests repeated the item into mid-August, some with the date shifted to "the 2d" or "the 31st ult."

Some Tennessee papers were openly approving. The Memphis Daily Appeal ran its account under the headline "Will They Never Learn," with the subhead "That Almost Certain Death Awalts [Awaits] Perpetration of the Crime?", and said the mob gave Wells "that punishment he so justly deserved." The Clarksville Weekly Chronicle wrote that "DYERSBURG had the hanging entertainment this week."

The Pulaski Citizen dissented, complaining that "nearly all the papers in Tennessee are busily excusing the mobs at Murfrcesboro [Murfreesboro], Dyersburg and e'sewhere [elsewhere]" on the ground that the courts were slow, and arguing that each lynching further demoralized the people. The governor's proclamation was reprinted in Tennessee and Nebraska papers in late August and early September.

The wire placed the hanging between twelve and one in the morning, while the Appeal gave that hour for the attack on Mrs. Childs and placed the lynching between 10 and 11 the next day, after a 4 a.m. arrest. The Appeal's Tennessee special gives the fuller sequence; both put the lynching on August 1. Several papers printed the victim's name as "Mike Walls" and the widow's as Childress, Childers or Fields, but the Tennessee reports and the governor's proclamation use Wells.

reader.title: Lynching of Mike Wells
bases: Wells was taken from a guard after his arrest and hanged in the Courthouse yard by 'an indignant mob' or 'the citizens' (A2, A7, A17), and the governor offered a reward for those who 'mobbed' him (A30).

Wells was hanged without trial by 'a mob of citizens of the town' (A17) or 'an indignant mob' (A7) as punishment for an alleged attempted outrage (A2, A7), and the governor treated the act as mob violence by offering a reward for the participants (A30, A33).

The Dyersburg wire (A2, A17), separate Cincinnati specials (A4), a Rutherford, Tenn., special to the Memphis Appeal (A7) and Governor Hawkins's later proclamation (A30, A33) agree that Wells was lynched at Dyersburg on Aug. 1, 1881.
